subject: Premium support ops exceptions & commitment path — DataHaven
messages:
From: Claire Wu <claire@datahaven.ai>
To: sergio_alvarez <sergio@redwood.ai>, ben_carter <ben@redwood.ai>
Cc: procurement@datahaven.ai
Date: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Questions on premium SLA packaging and exceptions

Thanks for taking a look — quick context: we’re evaluating Redwood for a core inference layer for our docs-embedding product. Procurement asked me to confirm how premium SLA and support packaging would apply to our model workload, specifically:

- How are uptime lanes defined (do you measure at API endpoint or per-dedicated-pool)?
- If we commit to a 12-month reserved capacity, what discount bands are available and how do volume triggers work (monthly cadence vs. annual true-up)?
- Can we get explicit language for ops-window exceptions (planned maintenance, regional failover windows) so our SREs can bake that into runbooks?
- Are there rollover credits for unused response-hour retainer or a mitigation credit model for maintenance windows?
- We also need clarity on multi-region failover credits and whether canary fallback to a lower-cost model would be treated as a SLA breach for billing/credits.

Attached: DataHaven-SLA-requirements.pdf (high-level requirements / expected peak qps).

Goal: get a short formal proposal we can attach to a Master Services Agreement. Ideally we’d like to see a few concrete packaging options (committed TCV bands + resulting uptime + response windows + annual discount).

Thanks,
Claire Wu
Head of Infrastructure
DataHaven Analytics

From: sergio_alvarez <sergio@redwood.ai>

Cc: ben_carter <ben@redwood.ai>, laura_bennett <laura@redwood.ai>, priyom_das <priyom@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Questions on premium SLA packaging and exceptions

Claire — thanks for the clear list, appreciate the attachment. High level responses below and we can lock numbers after a short sync / quick sizing call. I’ll flag the items where I want to loop legal/pricing (cc’d).

1) Uptime lanes: we measure committed uptime at the customer-facing model endpoint. For Dedicated pools we also report per-pool availability as an internal metric; SLA credits are computed against the endpoint uptime. Typical lanes we offer: 99.9%, 99.95%, 99.99% (we can publish percentile targets and token-based unit economics for each).

2) Discounts / volume triggers: we do a banded discount by committed monthly throughput (tokens and/or dedicated vGPU pool hours). Example bands: 0-5TB/mo (base list), 5-20TB/mo (-8%), 20-50TB/mo (-15%), 50TB+ (custom). Annualization/true-up: we support quarterly re-true-ups or an annual true-up depending on procurement preference. We can do stepped discounts that unlock when a rolling 30-day usage crosses thresholds.

3) Ops-window exceptions & maintenance: we have a defined Planned Maintenance window (usually a weekly 2-hour low-impact window by region) — planned windows are exempt from SLA credits if notified X days in advance. For unexpected regional failovers, we provide bridge credits depending on duration and whether fallback was to a degraded model (we treat a planned canary fallback as an operational mitigation, not an SLA breach, provided it follows the agreed rollback/canary policy). We should add explicit language around notification windows and nomination of your SRE contacts for escalation.

4) Rollover credits / retainer use: for retainer-based oncall or priority lanes, we offer monthly pools of response hours that can be rolled forward quarter-to-quarter up to a cap (e.g., 25% of monthly retainer). For longer unused periods we typically convert to service credits rather than cash refunds.

5) Multi-region & canary fallback: we can provide a failover credit schedule and a canary-fallback carve-out. If you enable automatic fallback to a compatible lower-cost model, we’ll not count those minutes as SLA breaches if the fallback is part of an agreed routing policy; if fallback occurs due to capacity constraints without prior routing policy, credits may apply.

Next steps I propose:
- I’ll attach a short pricing spreadsheet (SLA-pricing-draft.xlsx) with bands and sample pricing (attached).
- Ben and Laura — can you confirm if we want to propose a 12-month commit with a 10% first-year seniority discount and a sightline to firm pricing at 50TB+?
- Claire — are you available for a 30-min call next Tue/Wed to walk the vendor-side runbook and confirm the qps numbers in the attachment?

Thanks,
Sergio Alvarez
Director, Strategic Accounts
Redwood Inference

Attachment: SLA-pricing-draft.xlsx

Claire — quick follow with a couple practical commercial structures we’ve used for customers with similar profile: 

- Annualized support hours: instead of monthly retainer pulses, we can annualize the support retainer (e.g., 600 hours/yr) and amortize across months for predictable billing. This often reduces effective unit price and avoids month-to-month rollover noise.

- Ops-window exceptions: we recommend defining 4 annual maintenance windows (pre-scheduled) that are excluded from SLA calculations. Any additional planned maintenance is subject to mutual scheduling. Unexpected failovers are handled via a graded-credit ladder (first 30 mins = advisory, 30-240 mins = partial credit, >240 mins = full-tier credit).

- Pilot / bridge: propose a 3-month pilot with a capped credit pool (e.g., $Xk) to validate failover behavior and runbook. If you convert to an annual committed contract, we roll the pilot fee into the first invoice.

One practical ask from our side: the SE team needs a peak inference QPS estimate (and a 95th percentile token length). That will help us size whether a Dedicated pool is required or whether Hosted with reserved throughput fits — pricing and credits differ between those.

If you can provide a short vector: expected peak qps, average tokens per request, and whether inference is mainly streaming or single-response, we’ll firm up the spreadsheet numbers.

—Ben
Ben Carter
Principal Commercial Operations
Redwood Inference
